title: Use `Stream.peek` to log each employee as it passes a filtering and mapping pipeline, for auditing, without altering the elements. Explain what `peek` does, why it is an intermediate operation, and the caution about relying on it.
shortTitle: Audit each element flowing through a pipeline using peek without changing the data

s1_definition.profdef: `Stream.peek(consumer)` is an intermediate operation that performs a side effect on each element as it flows past — typically logging — and passes the element downstream unchanged. It exists mainly to observe or debug a pipeline, not to transform data.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a conveyor belt of account forms. peek is a CCTV camera over the belt that photographs each form as it goes by for the audit log, but it never changes or removes a form. The forms continue down the belt exactly as they were.
s1_definition.oneliner: `peek` lets you watch elements go by for logging or debugging without modifying them — it is a side-effect window, not a transformer.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `Stream.peek(consumer)` is an intermediate operation that performs a side effect on each element as it flows past — typically logging — and passes the element downstream unchanged. It exists mainly to observe or debug a pipeline, not to transform data.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a conveyor belt of account forms. peek is a CCTV camera over the belt that photographs each form as it goes by for the audit log, but it never changes or removes a form. The forms continue down the belt exactly as they were.

**One line to remember:** `peek` lets you watch elements go by for logging or debugging without modifying them — it is a side-effect window, not a transformer.

sections.s2_technical:
`peek(consumer)` applies the consumer to each element and then emits that same element to the next stage. It is an intermediate operation, so it is lazy — the consumer runs only as the terminal pulls elements through, and only for elements that actually reach the peek stage after earlier filters. For example `employees.stream().filter(e -> e.getSalary() > 1_000_000).peek(e -> log.info("passed filter: " + e.getName())).map(Employee::getName).collect(toList())` logs only the high earners because peek sits after the filter.

The classic use is debugging: dropping a peek between stages reveals exactly what each stage produces. It can also drive lightweight auditing, logging each element that survives a business filter.

The senior caution is important. peek is for observation; you should not rely on it for essential logic because an optimizing pipeline may skip peek when the result can be computed without visiting every element — for instance `stream.peek(...).count()` on some JDKs may not invoke peek at all if the count can be derived structurally. Side effects in peek must be non-essential and, in parallel streams, thread-safe. For real transformations use map; for terminal side effects use forEach.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a pipeline that filters high earners and extracts their names for a report. Compliance wants an audit trail showing which employees passed the high-earner filter, but the pipeline's output must stay exactly the list of names — the audit must not alter it.

This is exactly what peek is for — it sits after the filter, logs each employee who passed as an audit line, and hands the same employee onward to the mapping stage untouched.

The code defines `Employee`, a `HighEarnerReport` service using peek for audit, and a demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: four employees with a threshold of one million.

Step 1: The stream filters by salary; Rajesh at 1.2M and Sneha at 1.5M pass, Priya and Amit are dropped.

Step 2: peek runs only for the survivors, logging an audit line for Rajesh and one for Sneha, and passes each unchanged.

Step 3: map converts each surviving employee to its name.

Step 4: The collector gathers the names into the report output, Rajesh and Sneha, exactly as expected and unaffected by the peek.

```
INFO: AUDIT passed filter: Rajesh
INFO: AUDIT passed filter: Sneha
INFO: Report output (names only): [Rajesh, Sneha]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  [Rajesh 1.2M, Priya 0.9M, Sneha 1.5M, Amit 0.7M]
    │ filter(salary > 1M)
    ▼
  [Rajesh, Sneha]
    │ peek(log AUDIT)   ← side effect only, element unchanged
    │   "AUDIT passed filter: Rajesh"
    │   "AUDIT passed filter: Sneha"
    ▼ map(getName)
  ["Rajesh", "Sneha"]   ← output identical to without peek
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
peek is an intermediate operation that applies a side effect, usually logging, to each element as it flows past and then passes the same element downstream unchanged. It is designed for observing a pipeline, not transforming it. Because it is intermediate and lazy, the consumer runs only as a terminal pulls elements through, and only for elements that actually reach the peek stage, so a peek placed after a filter sees only the survivors.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I had a pipeline that filtered high earners and extracted their names for a report, and compliance wanted an audit trail of who passed the filter without changing the output. I dropped a peek right after the filter to log each passing employee, and the mapping and collection downstream produced exactly the same list of names as before.

The senior caution I always voice is that peek must only carry non-essential side effects. An optimizing pipeline can legally skip peek when it can produce the result without visiting every element — count is the classic case — so I never place business-critical logic in peek. For genuine transformation I use map, and for a terminal side effect over every element I use forEach; peek stays reserved for debugging and lightweight auditing.
